name: kepler.gl
maintainer: kepler.gl contributors (Uber origin, now Linux Foundation)
purpose: Web application and React component for exploratory geospatial visualisation of large datasets, with point, arc, hexbin, heatmap and trip layers, time playback and no-code layer configuration.
journalism_use_case: Exploring and presenting large location datasets without writing visualisation code: drop a CSV of hundreds of thousands of incidents in, configure a hexbin or time-animated trip layer, and see the pattern — then export the configuration for a published graphic.
pros: No-code layer configuration lets an analyst explore a large spatial dataset in minutes, which is where patterns are actually found — far faster than scripting candidate visualisations
Handles hundreds of thousands of points smoothly via deck.gl, well beyond what a Leaflet map manages
Time playback is directly useful for movement and sequence stories (flight paths, vessel tracks, incident progression)
MIT licensed with active development (pushed 2026-11-17) and Linux Foundation governance after its Uber origin
cons: Release line is in a long alpha (v3.3.0-alpha.22, 2026-11-16), so there is no current stable release to pin — awkward for production use
Heavy client-side application: large datasets need a capable machine, and embedding it in a story page adds substantial weight
Exploratory output is rarely publication-quality as-is; turning a kepler.gl view into a designed graphic is a separate step
277 open issues and a governance transition history, so direction is less predictable than a single-maintainer project
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 12,094 stars with 277 open issues, release v3.3.0-alpha.22 (2026-11-16), pushed 2026-11-17, MIT licence. The prolonged alpha release line is visible in the API data and is the main operational caveat.
assessment: Adopt it as an exploration tool rather than a publication tool — its value is letting an analyst see a large spatial dataset's structure quickly, which is hard to do any other way. For your profile the sensible workflow is kepler.gl to find the pattern, then a designed MapLibre or static graphic to publish it. Pin a specific alpha build if you embed it anywhere, since there is no stable release to rely on.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v3.3.0-alpha.22 (2026-11-16), 12,094 stars, 277 open issues. Same-day commits and frequent alpha releases under Linux Foundation governance; activity is clear, release stability is not.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Basemap tiles come from a configured provider with its own terms.
licence_restrictions: None material for the library. Default basemap configuration may point at a commercial provider requiring a token — check before publishing.
costs: No fee. Client-side compute. If the default basemap provider requires a token, those terms and costs apply (not priced here). Estimate.
privacy: Data can be loaded entirely client-side, so your dataset need not be uploaded anywhere — a genuine advantage over hosted visualisation services. Basemap tile requests go to the configured provider, disclosing viewport.
alternatives: QGIS for analytical rather than visual exploration
MapLibre with a custom build for publication-quality output
Datasette with a mapping plugin for lighter exploration of smaller datasets

name: Turf.js
purpose: Modular JavaScript and TypeScript library of geospatial operations — measurement, buffering, intersection, point-in-polygon, clustering, transformation — working on GeoJSON in the browser or Node.
journalism_use_case: Spatial computation in a published graphic or a JavaScript pipeline: compute which administrative district each incident falls in, buffer a pipeline route to show affected settlements, or calculate distances for an interactive the reader manipulates.
pros: Modular packages mean you import only the operations you need, keeping published graphics light — important for interactive stories on constrained connections
Working directly on GeoJSON matches the format newsroom spatial data actually arrives in, so there is no conversion step
MIT licensed with active maintenance (v7.4.0, 2026-08-03; pushed 2026-11-11) and a large community (10,550 stars)
Lets spatial logic live in the browser, so a reader-facing interactive can compute rather than only display
cons: Planar and spherical operation semantics differ across functions, and using the wrong one produces subtly wrong distances or areas — the same projection hazard as in any spatial work, surfaced differently
Performance degrades on large feature collections, so it is for computation over modest datasets, not corpus-scale spatial analysis (use geopandas or DuckDB spatial for that)
302 open issues and a non-semantic release tag alongside the version, so pinning needs attention
JavaScript-only, so it does not help a Python analysis pipeline
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 10,550 stars with 302 open issues, release v7.4.0 (2026-08-03), pushed 2026-11-11, MIT licence. Widely used in web mapping, which is well established in the ecosystem.
assessment: Integrate it where spatial computation belongs in the browser or a Node pipeline — chiefly for interactives where the reader's input drives a calculation. For your profile the caution is the same as for all spatial work: be explicit about whether you are computing on a plane or a sphere, and verify a sample of results against geopandas or QGIS before a computed figure is published. For analysis rather than presentation, use the Python stack.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-11, latest release v7.4.0 (2026-08-03), 10,550 stars, 302 open issues. Current commits with a 7.x release line from a community team.
privacy: Client-side or local computation with no network calls — data need not leave the browser.
alternatives: geopandas or DuckDB spatial for server-side and larger-scale computation
PostGIS for spatial SQL at scale
Shapely for Python-native geometry operations

name: titiler
purpose: Modular FastAPI application for dynamically serving map tiles from cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs and STAC items, with on-the-fly band math, rescaling and colour mapping.
journalism_use_case: Publishing satellite imagery interactively without pre-rendering tiles: serve a before-and-after pair of Sentinel scenes with a band-math index computed on request, so readers can pan and compare a damaged area themselves rather than looking at two static crops.
pros: Dynamic band math means you can publish an interactive vegetation or burn index without producing a tileset in advance — a materially shorter path from analysis to published graphic
Works directly against cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs and STAC catalogues, so it plugs into the pystac-based imagery workflow
MIT licensed with very active maintenance (release 2.4.1 on 2026-11-16, pushed 2026-11-17) and a clean tracker (25 open issues)
FastAPI-based and modular, so it is straightforward for a Python team to deploy and extend
cons: Dynamic tiling means a running server with compute per request, so a story that goes viral becomes a cost and capacity question — unlike PMTiles' static approach
Release-object and tag divergence (2.4.1 release against a v0.25.0 tag) makes version tracking confusing
Requires understanding of raster band semantics and rescaling to produce a correct image, so a misconfigured deployment publishes a misleading picture
Narrow use case: it serves raster imagery, and most newsroom maps are vector
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,208 stars with 25 open issues, release 2.4.1 (2026-11-16), pushed 2026-11-17, MIT licence. Development Seed is an established geospatial engineering organisation, which is the relevant institutional context.
assessment: Integrate it where satellite imagery is the published artefact and interactivity matters — otherwise pre-render static images, which is cheaper and more robust. For your profile the planning point is capacity: a dynamic tile server behind a successful story is a scaling problem you will meet at the worst moment, so put a CDN in front and consider pre-rendering the specific views the story emphasises while leaving the dynamic path for exploration.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 2.4.1 (2026-11-16), 1,208 stars, 25 open issues. Same-day commits and a release within a day of the survey, under an established organisation.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Served imagery carries the provider's licence — commercial scenes often restrict redistribution, which publishing tiles would constitute.
licence_restrictions: Software permissive. The real constraint is imagery rights: publishing tiles of commercial satellite imagery is redistribution and usually requires specific permission.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure: a running server with compute per tile request plus egress — the cost scales with readership, unlike static tiles. Put a CDN in front. Estimate.
privacy: Your server serves the tiles, so no third-party provider sees reader requests — but your server does, so reader-request logging is a policy decision.
alternatives: Pre-rendered static images or PMTiles for most published imagery
QGIS exports for a one-off graphic
A commercial imagery platform's embed, accepting third-party dependency and reader exposure
blockers: Publishing commercial satellite imagery as tiles is redistribution and usually needs explicit permission

name: Alaveteli
purpose: Platform for running a public freedom-of-information request site: users submit requests to public bodies, correspondence is published automatically, and the resulting archive of requests and responses becomes a public resource.
journalism_use_case: Two uses: running a national FOI platform (as WhatDoTheyKnow and its many deployments do), and mining an existing deployment's archive — because every request and response is public, an Alaveteli instance is a searchable corpus of what public bodies have disclosed and refused.
pros: Publishing requests and responses by default creates a public accountability record, which is a genuinely different model from private FOI correspondence and produces a reusable archive
Deployed nationally in many countries, so the model is proven and the codebase handles real administrative complexity (public-body registers, refusal handling, appeals)
AGPL-3.0-or-later (licence verified in session 1 by reading the text) with mySociety's long institutional record in civic technology
The archive of an existing instance is immediately useful to a journalist without running anything: searching prior requests shows what a body has already disclosed
cons: Running an instance is a substantial undertaking: a Rails application plus mail handling, a public-body register to maintain, and moderation of user-submitted content including the legal exposure that brings
Publishing everything by default is the wrong model for a journalist's own sensitive requests, since it tells the target and competitors what you are asking
Maintenance is steady rather than brisk, and the deployment documentation assumes operational competence with Rails and mail infrastructure
Jurisdiction-specific configuration (bodies, laws, timescales) is significant work for a new country deployment
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: session 1's a1disc/notes.md independently recorded 'alaveteli AGPL-3.0-or-later' after reading the licence text, resolving a NOASSERTION. The platform's national deployments are documented by mySociety and constitute strong evidence that the model works at scale.
assessment: For your profile the realistic value is as a source rather than software: mine existing Alaveteli instances for what bodies have already disclosed before filing your own requests, which saves time and reveals the body's refusal patterns. Running an instance makes sense only as a civic-infrastructure project, not as newsroom tooling, and the publish-by-default model is actively wrong for a sensitive investigation — file those directly and privately.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived, with mySociety's continued institutional maintenance. Release cadence is modest; the platform is mature and deployments are long-lived. Session 1 verified the licence by reading the text.
licence: AGPL-3.0-or-later (verified in session 1 by reading the licence text, resolving a GitHub NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: Request and response content published on an instance is public; the underlying disclosed documents remain subject to the releasing body's terms.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0-or-later: a modified public instance obliges source publication — which, for a platform whose purpose is public deployment, is a real obligation rather than a theoretical one.
costs: No software fee. Running an instance: a Rails host, a database, reliable mail infrastructure and moderation staff time — the staff cost dominates and is ongoing. Not a small commitment. Estimate.
privacy: Deliberately public: requests and responses are published, and requester names are typically visible. This is the point of the platform and the reason not to use it for a sensitive journalistic request.
alternatives: Froide for the German-lineage equivalent with a similar model
MuckRock for a US FOI platform with both public and private request options
Filing requests directly and privately for sensitive investigations
blockers: Publish-by-default model is unsuitable for sensitive journalistic requests

name: Froide
purpose: Django-based freedom-of-information platform managing requests to public bodies, correspondence tracking, deadlines, publication of responses and a public-body database, powering FragDenStaat and similar sites.
journalism_use_case: The German-lineage FOI platform, and like Alaveteli valuable to a journalist primarily as an archive: FragDenStaat's public corpus of requests and responses is a searchable record of German administrative disclosure, which is a research resource before it is a tool.
pros: Deadline and correspondence tracking is more developed than in some alternatives, reflecting the procedural detail of German FOI law — useful if you file many requests
Django-based, which fits a Python newsroom stack better than a Rails deployment
Powers a substantial national platform (FragDenStaat), so it is proven in production with real administrative complexity
Open-source with an active civic-tech maintainer in OKF Deutschland
cons: Strongly oriented to German law and administrative practice, so deploying it elsewhere means substantial adaptation of bodies, deadlines and legal references
Like Alaveteli, publication-oriented by default, which is the wrong posture for a sensitive journalistic request
Self-hosting is a real Django deployment with mail handling and moderation obligations — a civic-infrastructure project rather than newsroom tooling
Documentation and community are substantially German-language, which is a friction for a non-German-speaking team
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived under OKF Deutschland's maintenance. FragDenStaat's operation is the production evidence; I verified no non-German deployment.
assessment: Relevant chiefly if you work on Germany, where FragDenStaat's archive is a genuine research asset and worth searching before filing. As software, the same conclusion as Alaveteli applies: running an FOI platform is civic infrastructure, not newsroom tooling, and the publish-by-default model conflicts with investigative practice. For your profile, use the archives and file sensitive requests yourself.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under institutional maintenance by OKF Deutschland, with steady rather than frequent development. Classified stable-low: a mature platform supporting an operating national service.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Published request and response content is public; disclosed documents remain subject to the releasing body's terms.
licence_restrictions: Permissive as published; confirm the licence file before redistribution.
costs: No software fee. Running an instance: Django host, database, mail infrastructure and moderation staff — the staff cost dominates. Estimate.
privacy: Publication-oriented by default, like Alaveteli; requests and responses are public.
alternatives: Alaveteli for the more widely deployed platform
FragDenStaat's public archive as a research source without running anything
Direct private requests for sensitive investigations
blockers: German-law orientation; publish-by-default unsuitable for sensitive requests

name: warn-scraper
purpose: Command-line scraper that collects WARN Act notices — statutory advance notifications of US plant closings and mass layoffs — from every state agency that publishes them, normalising them into a single dataset.
journalism_use_case: A working model of sustained public-records collection: layoff notices are published by fifty separate state agencies in fifty formats, and this consolidates them into one dataset that supports both local stories ('which employers in this county are cutting jobs') and national analysis.
pros: Solves a real and recurring local-news need across every US state, and the consolidated dataset is directly usable for both local and national reporting
Demonstrates the pattern worth copying: one scraper per jurisdiction, normalised into a shared schema, released as a package — the right architecture for any multi-jurisdiction records problem
Licence resolved: Apache-2.0 (read from the licence blob; GitHub reports NOASSERTION, and session 1 independently recorded Apache-2.0)
Actively maintained with a frequent release cadence (1.2.178, 2026-10-26; pushed 2026-11-13) by an academic data-journalism programme
cons: State agency sites change constantly, so 73 open issues against 45 stars mostly reflects per-state breakage — the maintenance burden of multi-jurisdiction scraping is the honest lesson here
US only, so it is a template rather than a resource for other countries
Small community, and the long-term dependency is on one academic programme's funding
Normalisation across fifty formats necessarily loses state-specific detail, so for a single-state story the original source may be better
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 45 stars with 73 open issues, release 1.2.178 (2026-10-26), pushed 2026-11-13, SPDX NOASSERTION with the licence blob read 2026-11-17 confirming Apache-2.0 (Copyright 2025 Big Local News) — consistent with session 1's independent reading. The high issue-to-star ratio is itself the evidence about per-jurisdiction scraper maintenance.
assessment: Directly useful if you cover the US, and more broadly useful as a template: the one-scraper-per-jurisdiction-into-a-shared-schema pattern is how you build a durable public-records asset, and the open issue count is an honest warning about the ongoing cost. For your profile I would copy the architecture for whichever multi-jurisdiction records matter in your region, and budget continuing maintenance rather than treating collection as a one-off project.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-13, latest release 1.2.178 (2026-10-26), 45 stars, 73 open issues. Very frequent releases (a 1.2.178 version number reflects continuous per-state fixes) under an academic programme; the backlog is intrinsic to scraping fifty changing sites.
licence: Apache-2.0 (licence blob read 2026-11-17, Copyright 2025 Big Local News; GitHub reports NOASSERTION — also independently recorded in session 1's a1disc/notes.md)
model_or_data_licence: Collected notices are US state government records, generally freely usable.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. Collected public records carry no material restriction in this case.
costs: No fee. Negligible compute. The real cost is maintenance of per-state scrapers if you fork or extend it. Estimate.
privacy: Scrapes public government sites; no personal data beyond what the notices themselves contain (employer names and layoff counts, sometimes with contact details).
alternatives: Copying the architecture for your own jurisdictions — the more transferable use
Scrapy for building equivalent collectors from scratch
openstates-scrapers as another multi-jurisdiction public-records collection model

name: news-homepages
purpose: Toolkit and running archive that captures screenshots, full-text extracts, accessibility reports and hyperlink data from hundreds of news homepages on a schedule, publishing the results openly.
journalism_use_case: Studying editorial judgement over time: which stories a publication led with, how long a story stayed on the homepage, and how coverage differed across outlets on a given day — questions about media behaviour that require a systematic homepage archive nobody otherwise keeps.
pros: Captures a record that genuinely does not exist elsewhere: homepage prominence over time is editorial evidence, and it disappears within hours if not captured
Publishes the archive openly, so the research value is available without running anything — a rare and generous model
GPL-3.0 with very active maintenance (0.0.124 released 2026-11-16, pushed the same day) by a well-known data journalist
Multi-modal capture (screenshot, text, links, accessibility) means several kinds of analysis are possible from one archive
cons: Narrow analytical scope: it answers questions about homepage prominence, which is a specialised interest even within media research
Capture is of the homepage as the capturing machine saw it, so personalisation, geography and A/B variation all affect what is recorded — a methodological caveat for any comparison
Small project (163 stars, 28 open issues) dependent on one maintainer, though the published archive persists independently
Storage grows continuously, so self-hosting a long-running capture is a real commitment
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 163 stars with 28 open issues, release 0.0.124 (2026-11-16) with same-day push, GPL-3.0. The maintainer is an established figure in data journalism and the archive is published openly, which is verifiable from the project site.
assessment: Use the published archive rather than running your own capture unless you need outlets it does not cover — the research value is available for free and the storage commitment is someone else's. For your profile the interesting application is comparative: documenting that a state-aligned outlet led with a particular framing for days while independent outlets did not is a concrete, archived finding about editorial behaviour, and this is one of very few sources that supports it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 0.0.124 published the same day, 163 stars, 28 open issues. Frequent releases reflecting continuous operation of the capture pipeline.
model_or_data_licence: Captured homepage content remains the publishers' copyright; the archive is published for research use.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 on the toolkit. Republishing captured homepage screenshots raises publisher copyright, which is a fair-dealing judgement rather than a licence question.
costs: No fee to use the published archive. Self-hosting capture: continuous browser automation plus growing storage — a real and open-ended commitment. Estimate.
privacy: Captures public homepages; no personal data. Your own capture would be visible to the publishers as automated traffic.
alternatives: Internet Archive captures for ad-hoc historical homepage lookups
shot-scraper plus git for capturing a small set of homepages yourself
Media Cloud for article-level rather than homepage-level coverage analysis

name: git-history
purpose: Tool that analyses the history of a file tracked in git — typically a scraped data file committed on a schedule — and converts it into a SQLite database of versions and item-level changes.
journalism_use_case: The analysis half of git-scraping: once shot-scraper or a cron job has been committing a government dataset daily for months, git-history turns that commit log into a queryable record of every change — when a row appeared, changed value, or was quietly deleted.
pros: Converts a git history into item-level change records, which is exactly the question journalists ask of official data: what changed, when, and what disappeared
Completes the git-scraping pattern into something analysable, turning a monitoring habit into a dataset with provenance built in
Apache-2.0 and composes with Datasette, so the resulting database is immediately browsable and shareable
Small, focused tool that does one thing clearly
cons: Dormant-adjacent: release 0.7 and last push both 2025-12-21, nearly a year before this survey — a small tool, but its development has stopped
Only useful if you have already been committing data on a schedule, so the value depends on a habit established months earlier — the tool cannot recover history you did not capture
Assumes a reasonably stable file structure: a scraped file whose schema changes will produce confusing item histories
Small community (228 stars, 21 open issues)
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 228 stars with 21 open issues, release 0.7 (2025-12-21) with the last push the same day, Apache-2.0. The git-scraping pattern it supports is documented by the maintainer and widely adopted in data journalism.
assessment: Adopt the pattern immediately even if you use the tool later — the important action is to start committing the datasets you care about on a schedule now, because you cannot reconstruct a history you did not capture. git-history then makes that archive analysable. Its stalled development is low risk for a tool of this size, and the Datasette pairing means the output is useful to non-engineers.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2025-12-21, latest release 0.7 published the same day, 228 stars, 21 open issues. Eleven months since any activity on a small, complete tool. Classified stable-low rather than dormant given its narrow scope and minimal dependency surface.
privacy: Operates on local git repositories; no network calls. Note that if the scraped data repository is public, the monitored datasets and their history are public too.
alternatives: Writing SQL against the git log yourself for bespoke change analysis
EDGI web-monitoring-diff for HTML page diffs rather than structured data
Datasette to publish the resulting change database
